quote: Welches sind die wahrscheinlichsten Werte von $k_1, k_2, \ldots$ d.h. der Funktion $k_l$?
english: What are the most probable values of $k_1, k_2, \ldots$, i.e. of the function $k_l$?
topic: Statistical mechanics: deriving the most probable velocity distribution of molecules via Lagrange multipliers, then asking for the most probable distribution of an ensemble of systems over distributions, with an analogy to drawing black and white grains of sand, and a closing plan to study collision forces in Mie–Born electrodynamics.

triage.modern_statement: Take N molecules spread over cells l = 1, 2, … of velocity space, with k_l molecules in cell l. Hilbert asks for the occupation numbers {k_l} that maximise the number of microstates W = N!/∏ k_l!, given the constraints Σ k_l = N and Σ k_l ε_l = E. In modern terms this is the 'most probable distribution' problem of classical statistical mechanics. Maximising ln W with Lagrange multipliers gives the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution k_l ∝ exp(−β ε_l). The page goes on to ask the matching ensemble question: what is the most probable, or mean, distribution over distributions.
triage.answered_by: Ludwig Boltzmann, in his 1877 combinatorial paper: Lagrange-multiplier maximisation of the number of complexions gives the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. The ensemble/mean-value version was later made rigorous by C. G. Darwin and R. H. Fowler in 1922–23 (the Darwin–Fowler method), which showed that the mean values agree with the most probable ones. This is textbook material, not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or his 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Finding the most probable distribution of occupation numbers with Lagrange multipliers for the particle-number and energy constraints goes back to Boltzmann's 1877 paper.
Standard derivation: the most probable configuration (n_i molecules at energy level ε_i) is found with Lagrange multipliers for the two constraints, giving the Boltzmann distribution.

In Boltzmann's 1877 combinatorial work, the distribution function itself became a random variable (a macrostate) with its own probability distribution. This is the 'distribution over distributions' idea on Hilbert's page.
Darwin and Fowler (1922–1923) developed a method that derives distribution functions from mean values. It reproduces the most-probable-value result exactly, without approximations.

triage.why: The question asks for the most probable occupation numbers of molecular velocity cells, which is the classical Boltzmann problem; the page itself says the solution comes from Lagrange multipliers. Boltzmann solved it in 1877 and it is now standard textbook material. Darwin and Fowler settled the follow-up question of most probable versus mean values over an ensemble in 1922–23. Hilbert was evidently working through known statistical mechanics, likely for lectures or his physics studies, rather than posing a new problem. I found no evidence that it is one of his published problems. Inferences: the exact date of the note and how directly it ties to his later lectures are not established by the sources.
